meta.blurb: Priya is twenty-four, and her first full pay has just arrived. Her neighbour Mr Okafor, a retired shopkeeper, offers her one idea each week for a year. By the end she has money rules of her own, written for her own life.
meta.bible: Priya: a young woman of about twenty-four who has just started her first full-time job at a small design studio in a city; curious and careful. Her pay is 2,400 dollars a month after tax and her rent is 900 dollars. Mr Okafor: her retired neighbour, a shopkeeper for thirty years on Mill Street; patient, warm and practical; he shares one idea each week for a year, on Sunday evenings on his balcony. They talk on his balcony and in her kitchen over one year, from February to the next January. Mrs Okafor, whose first name is Ada: his wife, who kept the shop's accounts; calm and exact. Marta: Priya's colleague at the studio; generous, fun, always spending. Dev: Priya's younger brother, a student. Ms Lin: Priya's manager at the studio. Leo: Priya's partner. Tomi: a nineteen-year-old intern who joins the studio in the autumn and is the younger friend at the end. Priya's mother lives in another town. Places: the studio, Mill Street, the city. Money is counted in dollars, but every idea works in any country. Key terms: Interest, Compound interest, Inflation, Emergency fund, Credit, Index fund, Diversification, Insurance, Budget, Needs, Wants. No real people, companies, products or investments are named. Numbers are simple examples, not predictions: 4 dollars a day for 30 days is 120 dollars; 100 dollars growing at 5 in 100 each year is about 163 dollars after ten years; a yearly fee of 1 in 100 on 10,000 dollars is 100 dollars. Priya's plan: needs 1,500 dollars a month, wants 500, future 400 (at first laptop 60 and general savings 340; then cushion 200 and card payment 140 until the card is paid; later deposit, retirement plan and a trip fund). Later facts: the studio's retirement plan takes 100 dollars from Priya and adds 50; Ms Lin gives her a raise of 100 dollars a month after her animation course; Dev, who repays 200 dollars early; Ada kept the shop's accounts and chose its insurance; Mr Okafor's lemon tree grew from a seed on his balcony. Her goals: a laptop of 600 dollars by December, a home deposit in about five years, time to care for her mother in the far future. Priya's debts: a card balance of 300 dollars at 22 in 100 a year and a student loan at about 4 in 100 a year. This book is general information and is not personal financial advice. Voice and tone: kind, practical and calm; one clear idea per page; never promises riches; honest about risk and about what depends on the country and the person.

beats.scene: Priya holds her first pay slip at a small kitchen table
beats.summary: Priya, twenty-four, receives her first full pay and does not know what to do with it.

beats.scene: Priya listens to Marta, Dev and her mother, who all talk at once
beats.summary: Friends and family give Priya three different pieces of advice, and she feels more confused.

beats.scene: Mr Okafor waves to Priya from his balcony with a cup of tea
beats.summary: Her neighbour Mr Okafor, a retired shopkeeper, offers to share one idea about money each week for a year.

beats.scene: Mr Okafor hands Priya a plain blue notebook across the balcony wall
beats.summary: Mr Okafor sets one condition: Priya must test each idea in her own life and write down what happens.

beats.scene: A small corner shop on Mill Street with crates of fruit outside
beats.summary: In thirty years of keeping a shop, Mr Okafor saw that people with the same pay lived very different lives.

beats.scene: Mr Okafor taps a coin on the table in front of Priya
beats.summary: Money is a tool that buys choices and time, not a score to win.

beats.scene: Two coins on a table, one beside a small alarm clock
beats.summary: Money also buys time: savings let you rest, learn or change direction.

beats.scene: Priya sits on her bed with her notebook open on her knees
beats.summary: Priya thinks about which choices she wants: leaving a bad job, helping her mother, seeing the world.

beats.scene: Mr Okafor and Priya sit on the balcony with two cups of tea
beats.summary: Mr Okafor says he is a neighbour, not an expert, and that money rules differ from country to country.

beats.scene: Priya writes the word worried at the top of a clean page
beats.summary: Priya writes down her pay, her rent and one honest word for how money makes her feel.

beats.scene: A paper napkin with a large question mark drawn on it
beats.summary: Mr Okafor asks what Priya's money is for, because money without a purpose is only a number that disappears.

beats.scene: Priya writes three short lines on a notepad, each with a small drawing
beats.summary: Decide what money is for by writing one goal for the near, middle and far future.

beats.scene: A page with three drawings: a laptop, a small house and a train
beats.summary: Priya's goals are a laptop within the year, a home deposit in about five years, and time to care for her mother one day.

beats.scene: Priya writes six hundred dollars and December beside the laptop drawing
beats.summary: A goal needs an amount and a date: 600 dollars by December, ten months away, is 60 dollars a month.

beats.scene: A young Mr Okafor stands proudly beside a second-hand fridge in a small shop
beats.summary: Mr Okafor's first goal was a second-hand fridge for his shop, and he saved for eight months to buy it.

beats.scene: A pencil and an eraser beside the three goals in the notebook
beats.summary: Goals may change as life changes, so write them in pencil and review them.

beats.scene: Marta shows Priya a phone screen with a beach hotel and a high price
beats.summary: Marta invites Priya on an expensive weekend away, and Priya opens her notebook before she answers.

beats.scene: Priya smiles and shakes her head as Marta holds out a leaflet
beats.summary: Priya says no this time and suggests a cheap picnic; Mr Okafor tells her that not now is not the same as never.

beats.scene: Three small jars on a shelf, each with a handwritten label
beats.summary: Each goal gets its own named place for its money, so that it does not melt into everyday spending.

beats.scene: Priya sticks her page of three goals on the wall above the kitchen table
beats.summary: Priya sticks the page above her table and feels lighter.

beats.scene: Priya writes a spending list in her notebook at the kitchen table
beats.summary: Find out where your money goes by writing down every spending for one month.

beats.scene: A phone notes list beside an envelope stuffed with small paper receipts
beats.summary: Priya starts her record: a running note on her phone and an envelope in her bag for receipts.

beats.scene: Mr Okafor behind his shop counter counts coins into a small tray
beats.summary: Mr Okafor says that counting his stock every week taught him the truth about his shop.

beats.scene: Priya empties her purse onto the table and counts a few coins
beats.summary: Cash is the hardest spending to track, so Priya writes each purchase down before she leaves the shop.

beats.scene: Marta peers at Priya's phone note during a lunch break at the studio
beats.summary: Marta sees the list and admits she has no idea where her own pay goes.

beats.scene: Priya sorts receipts into piles on her kitchen table
beats.summary: At the end of the month Priya sorts everything into piles and adds each pile up.

beats.scene: A hand drops coins into a jar labelled with a coffee cup
beats.summary: Small, regular costs add up: four dollars a day is 120 dollars a month.

beats.scene: Priya holds a coffee cup and ticks a few lines in her notebook
beats.summary: Priya asks which coffees she truly enjoyed, keeps those and makes the rest at home, saving about 80 dollars.

beats.scene: A chart with one bar for pay in and one for money out
beats.summary: The gap between what you earn and what you spend is what builds everything else.

beats.scene: Priya draws her own two bars, and the gap is small
beats.summary: Priya's own gap is only about 200 dollars, but now she knows its true size and can work on it.

beats.scene: A kitchen table with three small boxes labelled needs, wants and future
beats.summary: Divide spending into three groups: needs, wants and your future.

beats.scene: Priya sorts a month of receipts into three labelled boxes on her table
beats.summary: Priya sorts a month of spending into the boxes: needs 1,500 dollars, wants 700, and only about 200 for her future.

beats.scene: Priya holds a coat and a phone, unsure which box they belong in
beats.summary: Some things sit between the boxes: the plain, working version is a need and the upgrade is a want.

beats.scene: Three boxes on the table, the future box now fuller than the others
beats.summary: Priya moves 200 dollars from wants to her future: needs 1,500, wants 500, future 400.

beats.scene: Priya smiles as she circles a small amount labelled fun in her notebook
beats.summary: A good plan is not a punishment, so leave some money for fun.

beats.scene: A shop customer counts coins at the counter beside an untouched cake
beats.summary: Mr Okafor tells of a customer who cut every treat at once, gave up after three weeks and overspent.

beats.scene: A phone screen shows a transfer to a savings account on pay day
beats.summary: Move money to savings automatically on pay day, before you can spend it.

beats.scene: Priya taps her phone to schedule two transfers for pay day
beats.summary: Priya sets up the transfers, 60 dollars to a laptop account and 340 to savings, and feels odd when the balance first drops.

beats.scene: A single page headed budget with three short columns
beats.summary: The three boxes make a budget: a plan for each month, written on one page.

beats.scene: Priya looks at three growing balances on her phone and smiles
beats.summary: After a month the plan works: Priya did not miss the 400 dollars, and the balances grew.

beats.scene: A bicycle with a bent back wheel leans against a wall in the rain
beats.summary: A bicycle wheel breaks on a rainy morning and the repair costs 180 dollars.

beats.scene: Priya taps her phone to pay the repair shop from her savings account
beats.summary: Priya pays the 180 dollars from her new savings; without them she would have used her card and borrowed at a high rate.

beats.scene: A broken umbrella lies beside a bill on a rainy doorstep
beats.summary: Unexpected costs will come, so you need a cushion of savings set aside for emergencies.

beats.scene: A repairman bends over a broken fridge in a shop while Ada watches
beats.summary: In a hot July, Mr Okafor's cushion let him mend the shop's broken fridge the same day and lose nothing.

beats.scene: Priya fills a calendar with twelve small boxes and ticks the first
beats.summary: Aim for a few months of basic costs, and begin with one month.

beats.scene: A calendar with four months crossed off and a small flag on the fifth
beats.summary: At 340 dollars a month, one month of basic costs, 1,500 dollars, will take about four months, so Priya circles the date.

beats.scene: A notebook list headed emergencies beside a list headed not emergencies
beats.summary: Priya lists what counts as an emergency (a lost job, an urgent repair, a medical bill) and what does not (a sale, a holiday).

beats.scene: A locked box on a shelf beside a small emergencies sign
beats.summary: Keep the emergency money safe, separate and easy to reach.

beats.scene: Priya moves a small amount back into the cushion account on her phone
beats.summary: Using the cushion for a real emergency is what it is for; afterwards, refill it before other goals.

beats.scene: Priya watches a small number grow on her savings screen
beats.summary: Start small, because a steady habit matters more than a large amount.

beats.scene: A stack of bills grows beside a small clock
beats.summary: Interest is the price of borrowing, and the longer you borrow the more you pay.

beats.scene: A thousand-dollar note with a small meter beside it showing two hundred dollars
beats.summary: Borrow 1,000 dollars at 20 in 100 a year, pay nothing back, and the bill grows by about 200 dollars in the first year.

beats.scene: A card statement with a very small minimum payment circled in pencil
beats.summary: Paying only the minimum keeps a debt alive for years, because most of each payment goes to interest.

beats.scene: Two doors: one opens to a classroom, one to a shop of flashing signs
beats.summary: Some borrowing can be useful, but the rate and the purpose matter.

beats.scene: A shop screen offers four small payments beside a much larger full price
beats.summary: Easy-payment offers make a price feel small; ask what the total cost is and what happens if you pay late.

beats.scene: Marta's phone shows a card balance of eighteen hundred dollars
beats.summary: Marta confesses that her card balance is 1,800 dollars and that she pays only the minimum each month.

beats.scene: Priya writes two debts on a page with their rates beside them
beats.summary: Priya lists her own debts: a card balance of 300 dollars at 22 in 100 a year, and a student loan at about 4 in 100.

beats.scene: Priya lists three debts on a page with their rates written beside them
beats.summary: If you owe money, list every debt and pay extra on the one with the highest rate first.

beats.scene: A scale: small savings on one side, a card on the other
beats.summary: Keep a small cushion first, then send the extra money to the debt with the highest rate.

beats.scene: A person ticks off a small debt on a long list and smiles
beats.summary: Another way is to clear the smallest debt first, and either method works if you keep going.

beats.scene: Priya crosses the last line off her card debt and smiles
beats.summary: After about three months of extra payments, the card balance reaches zero and Priya feels lighter.

beats.scene: A neighbour shows Priya a record of payments with a tick on each line
beats.summary: Lenders look at your record of paying on time, which can help you later, though rules differ by country.

beats.scene: Priya sets four reminders on her phone, each with a small bell
beats.summary: Good habits: set reminders, automate the minimum payments, apply for credit only when needed and read your own record.

beats.scene: A thick notebook with rows of ticks beside names on a shop counter
beats.summary: In his shop Mr Okafor kept a book of ticks for neighbours who paid later, and he trusted most those who paid on time.

beats.scene: Priya looks at a shiny car in a window, then at her bank screen
beats.summary: Spending to impress others uses up money without making you more secure.

beats.scene: A large shiny car parked outside a small shop beside an old bicycle
beats.summary: A customer with a huge car often asked to pay later, while the quiet customer on an old bicycle always paid in full.

beats.scene: A phone screen lists three monthly charges, two of them crossed out
beats.summary: Priya finds three forgotten monthly charges worth 35 dollars and cancels two of them.

beats.scene: Priya sticks a dated note on a green jacket's price tag
beats.summary: For any want over 50 dollars, wait seven days before buying; Priya tries the rule on a 90 dollar jacket.

beats.scene: Priya writes ninety dollars saved in her notebook beside the date
beats.summary: A week later Priya no longer wants the jacket, and she moves the 90 dollars to her laptop savings.

beats.scene: Priya laces up a pair of sturdy boots on a sunny morning
beats.summary: Spend freely on what you truly value: a good pair of boots worn every day costs little for each use.

beats.scene: A seed grows into a plant, then a tree, across a row of pots
beats.summary: Time is the saver's friend, because growth can build on earlier growth.

beats.scene: A tall lemon tree in a big pot beside a tiny pot
beats.summary: Mr Okafor's lemon tree grew slowly at first and then faster, as money that earns interest can when it is left alone.

beats.scene: Priya works out a sum on paper while Mr Okafor watches
beats.summary: 100 dollars growing at 5 in 100 each year is about 163 dollars after ten years.

beats.scene: Two small bars side by side, one a little taller than the other
beats.summary: Without growth on growth, 100 dollars would reach only 150 in ten years; the extra 13 dollars is growth on growth.

beats.scene: A curve on graph paper that rises slowly at first and then steeply
beats.summary: At the same rate, 100 dollars becomes about 265 after 20 years and about 432 after 30: most growth comes late.

beats.scene: Two paths start at different points and arrive at the same hill, one earlier
beats.summary: Starting early usually matters more than saving a little extra later.

beats.scene: Three small bars of different heights labelled two, five and seven
beats.summary: The rate matters too: 100 dollars becomes about 181 dollars in thirty years at 2 in 100, but about 432 at 5 in 100.

beats.scene: A jar receiving one coin each month beside a calendar of ten years
beats.summary: Adding 100 dollars every month for ten years puts in 12,000 dollars, which at 5 in 100 a year grows to a little over 15,000.

beats.scene: Priya compares two savings accounts on her phone, circling their rates
beats.summary: Priya checks the rate her savings account pays, finds a better one and checks that the money would be just as safe.

beats.scene: Priya draws a small tree with a date at its root
beats.summary: Priya writes the week's lesson in her notebook: begin now, add regularly and leave the money alone.

beats.scene: A basket of bread at a baker's with a higher price tag than before
beats.summary: Inflation means prices rise over time, so money kept unused buys less in the future.

beats.scene: Two price tags for the same loaf: an old one and a new one
beats.summary: In thirty years of shopkeeping, Mr Okafor saw the price of a loaf rise from about one dollar to about three.

beats.scene: A shopping basket holding bread, milk, a bus ticket and a bill
beats.summary: Inflation is measured by following the price of a typical basket of goods; the rate differs by country and by year.

beats.scene: A bundle of notes under a mattress shrinks into a smaller bundle
beats.summary: If prices rise 3 in 100 a year, 100 dollars kept in a drawer will buy only what about 74 dollars buys today after ten years.

beats.scene: A slow staircase going up beside a faster staircase
beats.summary: If savings earn 2 in 100 while prices rise 3 in 100, the money grows in number but shrinks in what it can buy.

beats.scene: Priya studies her pay slip while a long price list climbs the wall
beats.summary: If pay does not keep up with prices you are quietly poorer, so pay rises matter.

beats.scene: A heavy bag marked loan feels slightly lighter after many years
beats.summary: Inflation makes a fixed debt a little easier to repay over time, but that is no reason to borrow.

beats.scene: Priya moves cash from a kitchen drawer into a bank account
beats.summary: Priya moves 120 dollars of spare cash into her savings account, and learns which goals need safety and which need growth.

beats.scene: Priya holds an old receipt beside a new one and compares the totals
beats.summary: Priya compares a grocery receipt from February with a new one and finds that the same items cost a little more.

beats.scene: Mr Okafor and Priya stand at the balcony rail as the sun sets
beats.summary: Doing nothing is also a choice with a cost, and next week they will talk about investing.

beats.scene: Priya compares a sturdy jar of coins with a small garden growing plants
beats.summary: Saving is for safety and short goals, investing is for long goals and carries the chance of loss.

beats.scene: A small bakery with a sign showing a share cut from a larger pie
beats.summary: To invest is to put money into something that may earn more, such as a small piece of a business.

beats.scene: New wooden shelves stacked with goods as Ada smiles beside them
beats.summary: Mr Okafor's first investment was new shelves for his shop, and even that was a gamble.

beats.scene: An orchard with ripe fruit on the trees and a full basket below
beats.summary: An investment can reward you in two ways: its price may rise, and it may pay you regular income.

beats.scene: A seesaw with a small weight on one end and a big weight opposite
beats.summary: Higher possible gains come with bigger risks and bigger swings, and no one can offer high returns without risk.

beats.scene: A flat straight line beside a jagged rising line on graph paper
beats.summary: Savings rise in a smooth, small line; investments may rise further over many years but along a jagged line.

beats.scene: Two scales, one for money you could afford to lose and one for worry
beats.summary: Risk has two sides: how much loss your life can afford, and how much worry you can bear.

beats.scene: Priya watches a screen where a number drops from one thousand to nine hundred
beats.summary: Priya imagines her investment falling by a tenth in a month and asks herself honestly whether she would stay calm.

beats.scene: A ladder with four rungs labelled cushion, debt, goals and growth
beats.summary: Mr Okafor draws a ladder: a cushion first, then costly debt, then near goals, and only then long-term investing.

beats.scene: Priya colours in the first two rungs of a ladder in her notebook
beats.summary: Priya's cushion of one month is full and her card is paid, so she is standing on the third rung.

beats.scene: Eggs are shared between several baskets on a market table
beats.summary: Spread your money across many different things so that one failure does not ruin you.

beats.scene: A market stall piled with tomatoes under a dark stormy sky
beats.summary: One farmer who grew only tomatoes lost his whole harvest to a hailstorm, while a neighbour with five crops lost only one.

beats.scene: Marta points at a screen showing one company's price, rising sharply
beats.summary: Putting all your savings into one company because everyone is talking about it ties your whole future to a single business.

beats.scene: Three baskets on a market table labelled companies, kinds and countries
beats.summary: Money can be spread over many companies, over different kinds of investment and over different countries.

beats.scene: Many small coins drop into one large bowl that is shared by many hands
beats.summary: A fund pools money from many people to buy many things, and an index fund simply follows a large list.

beats.scene: A receipt showing units of a fund, with a manager at a desk behind
beats.summary: Money put into a fund buys units, each a tiny share of everything the fund owns, priced by the value of those holdings.

beats.scene: A long printed list of company names with a ruler beside it
beats.summary: An index fund copies a published list of many companies instead of picking winners, so it spreads money widely and usually costs little.

beats.scene: A runner with a heavy backpack labelled fees falls behind a runner without one
beats.summary: Some managers beat the market in some years, but studies in several countries find that most fall behind over many years once fees are counted.

beats.scene: Three jars labelled shares, bonds and mixed, each a different colour
beats.summary: Funds come in kinds: share funds usually swing most, bond funds usually swing less, and mixed funds blend the two.

beats.scene: Priya writes three words in her notebook: broad, cheap and simple
beats.summary: Mr Okafor will not tell Priya what to buy; she writes three things to look for: broad, low cost and simple to explain.

beats.scene: A small hand takes a tiny piece from a stack of coins each year
beats.summary: Fees matter, because a small yearly cost taken from your savings adds up over decades.

beats.scene: Two towers of coins labelled thirty years, one noticeably shorter than the other
beats.summary: Over 30 years 10,000 dollars growing at 5 in 100 becomes about 43,000, but with a yearly fee of 1 in 100 it becomes about 32,000.

beats.scene: A magnifying glass over the small print of a table of fees
beats.summary: Fees can hide in several places, so ask for the total yearly cost, in writing, in plain numbers.

beats.scene: A mountain-shaped graph with peaks and valleys rising overall across the years
beats.summary: Markets rise and fall, and a fall is only a loss on paper until you sell.

beats.scene: A long graph with a deep valley marked many years later
beats.summary: In the past, markets have sometimes fallen by a third or more and taken years to recover, and the future may differ.

beats.scene: A crowd runs past a road sign marked fear and greed while Priya waits
beats.summary: Fear and excitement push people to sell low and buy high, so decide your rules in advance.

beats.scene: Mr Okafor sits with his head in his hands over a falling graph
beats.summary: Mr Okafor admits that he once sold after a fall of a quarter and then watched the market recover without him.

beats.scene: Priya writes three lines headed my plan on a small card
beats.summary: Priya writes a three-line plan in a calm moment: how much she will invest, how often she will look, and what she will do if prices fall.

beats.scene: A phone lies face down beside a calendar with one day circled
beats.summary: Looking at prices every day makes small ups and downs feel big, so Priya plans to look only once a month.

beats.scene: A calendar with the same small amount placed in a jar every month
beats.summary: Investing a fixed amount each month spreads out the timing and builds a habit.

beats.scene: A row of jars labelled one, five and twenty years on a shelf
beats.summary: Money needed within a few years should not be placed where its value can fall.

beats.scene: A laptop in a shop window with a price tag and November calendar
beats.summary: Priya keeps her 570 dollars of laptop money in a safe account because she needs it within months, even though it earns little.

beats.scene: A young couple looks at a house sign beside a falling graph
beats.summary: A young couple who put their house deposit into shares saw it fall by a fifth the year before they wanted to buy, and had to wait.

beats.scene: A jar labelled five years, half filled with safe coins and half with seeds
beats.summary: For goals three to ten years away, many people keep a mix of safe and growth money and move toward safety as the date nears.

beats.scene: A distant sunny cottage at the end of a long winding road
beats.summary: Money for a goal thirty or forty years away has time to recover from falls, so it can usually take more risk.

beats.scene: Ms Lin hands Priya a leaflet at her desk at the studio
beats.summary: Ms Lin mentions that the studio's retirement plan adds money when an employee adds her own, and Priya has never read the leaflet.

beats.scene: Priya underlines lines on a leaflet with a pencil
beats.summary: Money an employer adds is like extra pay, so Priya checks how much it adds, the fees, where the money goes and when she can take it out.

beats.scene: Priya signs a form while Ms Lin watches with a smile
beats.summary: Priya joins the plan with 100 dollars a month from her future box, and the studio adds 50 dollars more.

beats.scene: A staircase: pay arrows grow longer, spending arrows stay shorter
beats.summary: When pay rises, spending tends to rise with it, so decide in advance to save a share of every raise.

beats.scene: Three jars labelled one, five and thirty years with a note under each
beats.summary: Priya sets up three jars by time: a safe one for near goals, a mixed one for the deposit and a long one for retirement.

beats.scene: A smiling stranger presses a glossy leaflet into Priya's hand as she steps back
beats.summary: Scams promise fast riches, press you to act now and ask for secrecy.

beats.scene: Marta wipes her eyes as she shows a group chat full of angry members
beats.summary: Marta's cousin lost his savings in a scheme that paid early members with the money of new ones, until new members stopped joining.

beats.scene: A pyramid of people with a tiny group on top, a crowd below
beats.summary: Such schemes need more and more new members; if each must find five more, twelve rounds would need more than 240 million people.

beats.scene: Priya reads a text message with a link and a small warning symbol
beats.summary: Messages that pretend to come from your bank and ask for codes or passwords are scams, so contact the real bank yourself.

beats.scene: A glossy leaflet promising guaranteed gains, with a small red cross drawn on it
beats.summary: Someone with a truly safe way to make huge profits would not need your money, so a guaranteed high return is a warning sign.

beats.scene: Priya types a company name beside the word complaints on her laptop
beats.summary: Before investing, check that the seller is registered where you live, search for complaints, ask for details in writing and wait a week.

beats.scene: A person on the phone while a friend gently holds her hand
beats.summary: Clever people are caught by scams too; anyone caught should tell the bank at once and report it, because speed can help and shame helps only the thief.

beats.scene: Tomi shows Priya an excited message on his phone at the studio
beats.summary: Tomi, the new nineteen-year-old intern, gets a message offering to double any money he sends within a day, and Priya helps him slow down.

beats.scene: Priya writes three questions on a yellow sticky note and hands it to Tomi
beats.summary: Priya gives Tomi three questions for any offer: who is this, who gains, and what happens if I wait a week; he deletes the message.

beats.scene: Priya turns on a two-step sign-in screen on her phone
beats.summary: Priya makes her accounts safer with a different long password for each one, a password manager and a second step when signing in.

beats.scene: Priya studies at a desk with a lamp and a stack of books
beats.summary: You can raise your income by building skills, and a higher income gives more room.

beats.scene: Priya reads a list of course names on a screen with one circled
beats.summary: Priya asks Ms Lin which skill the studio needs most, and learns that simple animation would make her more useful.

beats.scene: Priya types at a small desk under a lamp beside her course notes
beats.summary: Priya enrols in an eight-week animation course for 150 dollars and gives up some leisure to practise for three hours a week.

beats.scene: A small scale with a course fee on one side, coins on the other
beats.summary: If the new skill led to just 100 dollars more a month, the 150 dollar course would repay itself in under two months, though nobody can promise this.

beats.scene: A small moving logo on Priya's screen as Ms Lin looks on
beats.summary: Six weeks into the course, Priya animates a small logo for a client, and Ms Lin praises her in front of the team.

beats.scene: Mr Okafor plays the boss behind a desk while Priya reads her notes
beats.summary: Mr Okafor teaches the steps for asking for a raise: gather evidence, pick a calm moment and name a number.

beats.scene: Priya and Ms Lin sit across a small table with a notebook between them
beats.summary: Priya asks for a raise of 150 dollars a month; Ms Lin offers 100 dollars from next month and a review in six months.

beats.scene: Priya moves fifty dollars of her new raise into her deposit savings
beats.summary: Priya follows her rule: half of the new 100 dollars goes straight to her future box and half is hers to enjoy.

B1B2: Priya is twenty-four, and today she has received her first full-time pay. She is delighted, but she has no idea what a sensible person does with so much money.

Her colleague Marta tells her to enjoy the money, because life is short and pay day comes every month. Her brother Dev says she should buy a good phone, while her mother says she should save every single cent.
Mr Okafor lives next door, and for thirty years he ran a small shop. He offers to share one simple idea about money every week for a year, if Priya has the time to listen.
Mr Okafor has only one condition before he will begin his weekly lessons. Priya must test every idea in her own life and write down what happens in a plain notebook he gives her.
Mr Okafor tells her about his shop on Mill Street, where he served the same neighbours for thirty years. He noticed that two customers with the same pay could live very different lives.
Mr Okafor says that money is a tool and not a score. Its job is to give you choices, such as the freedom to say no to a job you dislike.

Mr Okafor adds that money does not only buy things, because it can also buy time. With some savings behind you, you can rest when you are unwell, learn something new or leave a job that makes you miserable.
That night Priya thinks about which choices she would most like to have. She would like the freedom to leave a bad job, to help her mother and, one day, to see other countries.
Mr Okafor says clearly that he is a neighbour and not a financial expert. Money rules differ from country to country, so Priya must check the details where she lives.
For homework Priya writes down her pay, her rent and one honest word for how money feels. The word she chooses is worried, and it looks bigger on the page than it did in her head.
Mr Okafor starts week two with a question: what is your money for? Priya cannot answer, and he explains that money without a purpose is just a number that slowly disappears.
Before any plan, Mr Okafor asks her to write down three goals: one for this year, one for five years and one for much later. A goal with a date and an amount is easier to reach than a hope.
Priya's first goal is to buy a laptop of her own before the end of the year. The second is a deposit for a home in about five years, and the third is time to care for her mother.
Mr Okafor shows her how to turn a wish into a plan. A laptop costing 600 dollars by December, ten months away, means setting aside 60 dollars each month.
Mr Okafor tells her that his first goal was a second-hand fridge for the shop. He saved for eight months, and the day it arrived he let himself have a small celebration.
Mr Okafor tells her to write the goals in pencil, because life will change and the goals may change with it. That is not failure, he says, but a sign that she is paying attention.
On Friday Marta invites her on a weekend at a beach hotel that costs 300 dollars. Priya feels the old urge to say yes at once, but she opens her notebook first.
Priya tells Marta that a 300 dollar weekend would swallow five months of her laptop savings. She suggests a picnic by the river instead, and Marta laughs and agrees.
Mr Okafor suggests keeping each goal's money in a separate place with its own name. When it all sits in one pile, he says, it quietly turns into everyday spending.
Priya sticks the page of goals on the wall above her kitchen table. It is only three lines, but she feels lighter, as though a vague worry has been given a shape.
Next, Mr Okafor asks her to write down everything she spends for one month, even the smallest things. You cannot change a habit that you cannot see.
On the first day Priya types every purchase into a note on her phone and puts the receipts in an envelope. It takes only a few seconds each time, and by the evening she has twelve small entries.
Mr Okafor says he counted his stock every Sunday night in the shop. The items he thought sold best were often not the ones that made him a profit.
By the second week Priya notices that her cash spending is the hardest to track. Small purchases vanish from memory, so she begins to write each one down before she leaves the shop.

At the end of the month Priya spreads the receipts across her kitchen table and sorts them into piles. Then she adds each pile up, and the totals are not what she expected.
At the end of the month, Priya sees that she spends four dollars on coffee every day, weekends included. That is 120 dollars in a month, more than she thought.
Priya asks herself which of the coffees she truly enjoys, and the answer is about one in three. She decides to keep those and to make the rest at home, which saves her about 80 dollars.
Mr Okafor draws two bars on a napkin, one for the money coming in and one for the money going out. The gap between them, he says, is the only money that can ever become savings.
Priya draws her own two bars, and the gap between them is only about 200 dollars. It is smaller than she hoped, but at least now she knows exactly how big it is.

Priya's story ends here, but yours is just beginning, so write your own rules to fit your life. This book is general information and not personal financial advice, so check the rules where you live and ask a professional if you need to.
C1C2: Priya had just turned twenty-four when the first full month's pay from her new job arrived in her account, a number larger than any she had ever owned. Delight came first, quickly followed by an uneasy suspicion that the money would vanish before she understood where it had gone. Like most people, she had never been taught how to manage it, and no one had thought to explain.

Within a day of the money arriving, the advice began to pour in from every direction. Her colleague Marta insisted that she should treat herself, her younger brother Dev urged her to buy a better phone, and her mother begged her to save every cent. Priya listened politely to all three, and found that she felt, if anything, more confused than she had been before.

Her neighbour Mr Okafor, who had run a small shop for most of his working life, noticed her worried face over the balcony wall and asked what the matter was. When she explained, he smiled and offered to share one plain idea about money each week for a year, on the condition that she would try each one for herself. It was the kind of offer that costs nothing, which is why she almost forgot to be grateful.

Mr Okafor's help came with a single condition, which he explained while he passed a plain blue notebook across the balcony wall. Every idea he offered, Priya was to test in her own life, and she was to write down honestly what happened, whether it worked or not. An idea that is never used, he said, is only conversation, and he had no wish to waste a year of Sundays on conversation.

For thirty years Mr Okafor had stood behind the counter of his shop on Mill Street, and he had watched the whole neighbourhood come and go with its shopping bags and its worries. What puzzled him was that two customers who earned exactly the same wages could end up in completely different places, one calm and secure and the other always anxious about the end of the month. The difference, he had slowly decided, was seldom intelligence or luck, and almost always the result of a handful of quiet habits.

The first idea, said Mr Okafor, is that money is a tool and never a scoreboard, so there is no prize for having the biggest number. What it really buys is choice, including the choice to say no to a job you dislike, to take a rest when you need one or to help someone in trouble. Priya wrote this down at the top of a clean page, which seemed a good place to begin.

Money buys things, he went on, but the more valuable thing it buys, if one is wise, is the time to decide for oneself. A person with some savings behind them can rest when they are ill, retrain when their work disappears or walk away from a job that is slowly making them miserable. Those who have nothing set aside, he observed, are often forced to accept whatever comes, and that is the opposite of choice.

That night, in her small flat, Priya tried to imagine which choices she would most like to own. The list came easily: the freedom to leave a job that made her unhappy, the means to help her mother without worry and, someday, the chance to see countries she had only known from photographs. She noticed that none of the items was an object, and that each of them could be reached only through time and planning.

Before they began, Mr Okafor was careful to say that he was a neighbour with a long memory and not a financial expert. Many of the rules about money, from taxes to pensions, differ from one country to another, and nothing he said could replace the facts that applied to Priya's own life. What he could offer, he promised, were the ideas that had proved themselves in his shop, in his family and in the lives of the people he had served.

For her first piece of homework, Priya wrote down her monthly pay of 2,400 dollars, her rent of 900 dollars and one honest word for the way money made her feel. The word she chose was worried, and it looked larger on the paper than it had ever looked inside her head. Mr Okafor would read it the following Sunday, and, to her surprise, she was looking forward to it.

At their second meeting Mr Okafor began with a question that sounded simpler than it was, namely what Priya's money was actually for. She opened her mouth, found that she had no answer to give, and closed it again with a small, embarrassed laugh. Money with no purpose, he said gently, is only a number on a screen, and a number with no purpose tends to leak away into the nearest sale.

Before any plan, said Mr Okafor, you must decide what the money is for, so he asked her to write three goals: one for within a year, one for about five years and one for the far future. Each goal should have an amount and a date, because a vague wish gives you nothing to measure while a clear target tells you how much to set aside. Priya's list was modest, but it was hers, and she noticed that it made her feel strangely lighter, as though a vague worry had at last been given a shape.

Her list, when it was finished, had three lines, each of them different in size, in distance and in how much it frightened her. The first was a laptop of her own, to be bought within the year, because the old one she used at home was lent by a friend and wheezed like a tired engine. The second was a deposit for a home in about five years, and the third, written in smaller letters, was the freedom to look after her mother one day without worrying about money.

A wish becomes a plan, said Mr Okafor, at the moment it acquires an amount and a date. Priya wrote beside her laptop that she needed 600 dollars by December, and the arithmetic was simple, since ten months of 60 dollars would do it. The sum looked small and calm on the page, which was precisely the effect he had been hoping for.

Mr Okafor's own first goal, he confessed, had been a second-hand fridge for the shop, without which he could sell nothing that spoiled in the summer heat. He saved for eight months, putting aside a little from every day's takings, and he remembered the afternoon it was delivered as one of the proudest of his life. The fridge was not glamorous, but it had a date and an amount attached to it, and that was why it arrived at all.

Write your goals in pencil, advised Mr Okafor, because a life is not a railway timetable and the destination you choose at twenty-four may well shift by thirty. Changing a goal is not a failure of nerve but a sign that you are paying attention to who you are becoming. What matters is that at every moment there is a goal, written down, with a number beside it.

On Friday Marta announced that a group from the studio was going to a beach hotel for the weekend, at a cost of 300 dollars each, and that Priya simply had to come. Priya felt the old reflex to say yes at once, the one that says everyone else is going and you will regret staying behind. Instead she asked for an evening to think, took out her notebook and looked at the three lines on the page.

Priya told Marta, kindly but without apology, that the weekend would swallow five months of her laptop savings, so this time the answer was no. She suggested a picnic by the river the following Saturday, which cost almost nothing, and was surprised when Marta agreed with delight. Mr Okafor, hearing the story, remarked that saying not now is very different from saying never, and that a goal merely lets you choose which yes is worth it.

In his shop, Mr Okafor said, he had kept separate tins for the rent, the suppliers and the repairs, and he had never once regretted the habit. Money that sits in a single pile has a way of dissolving into everyday spending, whereas money with a name and a purpose is hard to forget about or to raid. Priya decided that her laptop savings would have a name of their own, and a place of their own, from the very next pay day.

That evening Priya fixed the page to the wall above her kitchen table with two pieces of tape, where she would see it every morning with her breakfast. It was only three lines in pencil, and yet the effect was out of all proportion to its size. For the first time since the pay arrived, the money seemed to be pointing somewhere instead of simply sitting there.

Next came a month of honest observation, in which Priya was to record every single thing she spent, from rent to a bottle of water. Mr Okafor explained that you cannot improve a habit you cannot see, and that most people guess wrongly about where their money goes. She was not to judge herself while she did it, only to look, as a scientist looks at an experiment.

On the first morning Priya began a running note on her phone and kept an envelope in her bag for the paper receipts, and she was startled by how many entries a single day produced. A bus ticket, a bottle of water, a packet of gum, a sandwich and a charging cable all went onto the list before dinner. None of them seemed to matter, yet by evening she had spent more than she would have guessed, and the list was only beginning.

In the shop, Mr Okafor explained, he had counted the stock every Sunday night, and the figures had humbled him more than once. The goods he had been certain were selling best were often not the ones that earned him anything, while a dull box of batteries quietly paid for the electricity. Counting, he said, replaces what you believe with what is true, and only the second can be built upon.

By the second week Priya had discovered that cash was the hardest thing of all to follow, because a note or a coin handed over leaves no trace behind it. Twenty dollars would disappear from her purse on a Tuesday, and by Friday she could not say where it had gone. She solved the problem with a rule that was almost embarrassingly simple, which was to write down each purchase before she had even left the shop.

At lunch one day Marta spotted the growing list on Priya's phone and asked, with her usual curiosity, whether it was a shopping list or a confession. Priya explained the experiment, and Marta laughed, then stopped, then admitted in a lower voice that she had no idea where her own pay went each month. It was a small moment, but it showed Priya how many people carry the same quiet worry and never say so.

On the last evening of the month Priya spread her receipts and her phone notes across the kitchen table and sorted them into piles, as a gardener might sort seeds. One pile was housing, another food, another transport, and a stubborn pile of small things belonged nowhere at all. She added up each pile carefully with her pencil, and the totals were not at all what she had imagined.

At the end of the month, Priya was surprised to discover how much of her pay had gone on small daily treats, especially a coffee that cost four dollars. Multiplied by thirty days, that single habit came to a hundred and twenty dollars, which was more than she paid for her phone and her internet put together. Mr Okafor made no comment except to say that it was neither good nor bad, and that the only mistake was not to know.

Priya went through the month's coffees one by one and asked herself honestly which ones she had actually enjoyed, and the answer was about one in three. The rest had been bought out of habit, or boredom, or because the cafe happened to be on her way. She kept the good ones, made the others at home with a flask from the cupboard, and noticed with some satisfaction that the change would free about 80 dollars a month without making her feel deprived.

On a paper napkin Mr Okafor drew two bars, one tall for the money that came in each month and one for the money that went out. The gap between them, he said, is the whole secret, because that gap is the only source from which savings, investments and freedom can ever be drawn. If the second bar is taller than the first, he added, the difference must come from somewhere, and that somewhere is always debt.

That night Priya drew her own two bars on a page of the notebook, and the gap between them turned out to be only about 200 dollars. It was smaller than she had hoped, and for a moment she felt discouraged, until she realised that she had never before known the true size of anything. Now she had a number to improve, and a number can be improved in a way that a vague feeling never can.

To make the gap bigger without misery, Mr Okafor proposed that she sort her spending into three groups, namely needs, wants and her own future. Needs are the things she cannot do without, such as rent, food and transport, wants are the pleasures that make life enjoyable, and the future group is whatever she sets aside for her goals. There is no single correct split, he warned, because the right proportions depend on her pay, her city and her priorities.

At the kitchen table Priya sorted the whole month into the three boxes, and the result was both clear and a little sobering. Her needs came to 1,500 dollars, her wants to 700, and only about 200 dollars remained for her future, which was less than a tenth of her pay. It was the first time she had seen her life as a set of proportions, and the picture did not flatter her.

Some things, Priya found, refused to stay in one box, such as her phone, her winter coat and the bus pass that she sometimes swapped for a taxi. Mr Okafor offered a simple test, which was that the plain, working version of a thing is usually a need, while the upgrade, the brand or the convenience belongs in the wants. A coat keeps you warm, he said, but the third coat of the season has other jobs to do.

With the boxes in front of her, Priya went looking for 200 dollars to move from the wants to the future. She found it without much pain, by cooking at home more often, trimming the takeaway meals and passing over the small impulse purchases that she could not even remember afterwards. The needs stayed at 1,500, the wants fell to 500, and the future box rose from 200 to 400 dollars a month.

A plan that forbids all enjoyment will not last, Mr Okafor said, any more than a diet that forbids all food, and in both cases the failure usually arrives with a large and guilty splurge. Priya was therefore to set aside an amount for fun that she could spend without any guilt, as long as she stayed inside it. A plan she can live with every month, he added, is worth far more than a perfect one she abandons after two weeks.

Mr Okafor remembered a customer, a cheerful woman who bought lunch in his shop every day, who once decided to cut every pleasure from her budget at the same time. For three weeks she was a model of discipline, and then one tired Friday she abandoned the whole plan and spent more in a single afternoon than she had saved in a month. A plan that asks for perfection, he said, is a plan that has already planned its own failure.

Most people, said Mr Okafor, save what is left at the end of the month, and since little is ever left, they save nothing. He advised Priya to reverse the order by arranging for a fixed sum to move automatically into a separate savings account on the very day she was paid. Because the decision was taken once and the transfer happened without her, her willpower was no longer needed, which is exactly why it works.

It took Priya ten minutes at her phone to set up the transfers, 60 dollars to an account she named Laptop and 340 dollars to a general savings account. On the next pay day she watched her balance drop by 400 dollars before she had spent anything, and the feeling was oddly like losing something. Within a few days it had faded, and she had quietly adjusted to living on the smaller number, as one does to a new pair of shoes.

Put together, the three boxes made what Mr Okafor called a budget, a word that Priya had always associated with scolding and sacrifice. A budget, he insisted, is not a cage but a plan, drawn up before the month begins so that the money obeys your intentions instead of your moods. Hers fitted on a single page, with three boxes and one number inside each, and it was a good deal friendlier than she had feared.

A month later Priya sat down with her phone and looked at the three balances, which had grown by exactly the amounts she had planned. She had not missed the 400 dollars, she had not been short before the end of the month, and she had even enjoyed her fun money without a trace of guilt. What surprised her most was how little the change had hurt, compared with how large it had looked beforehand.

One wet Tuesday morning the back wheel of Priya's bicycle buckled against a kerb, and the repair shop quoted her 180 dollars to make it safe again. She needed the bicycle to reach the studio, so doing without it was not really an option, and the bill was not in anybody's budget. It was, she reflected, exactly the kind of small disaster that no plan ever seems to mention until it has already arrived.

Priya paid the 180 dollars from the savings account that she had opened only a month before, and the money left it with a small, painful tap. Without that account, she knew, the bill would have gone onto her credit card, where it would have grown more expensive every month until she paid it off. The savings had barely begun to exist, and yet they had already protected her from a bill that would have kept growing.

Life is certain to deliver surprises, said Mr Okafor, whether a broken phone, a repair bill, a sudden illness or the loss of a job, and the cost of these arrives when it is least convenient. A cushion of savings kept aside for such emergencies means that a setback remains a setback and does not become a crisis, because there is no need to borrow in a hurry or sell something at a loss. Of all the ideas he had to offer, he considered this one the most important to put in place early.

In a hot July, Mr Okafor recalled, the shop's fridge had died in the middle of the afternoon, with a delivery of milk and cheese still waiting on the pavement. His wife Ada, who kept the accounts, had insisted for years on a cushion of savings, so the repair was ordered and paid for before the evening and not a single item was lost. The neighbouring shop, which had no such reserve, spent a week waiting for credit and threw away most of its stock.

How much should the cushion hold, Priya wondered, and Mr Okafor replied that many experts suggest three to six months of basic living costs, though the right figure depends on her job and on who relies on her. A person with an unsteady income or a family to support may want more, and a person with steady pay and few responsibilities may be content with less. She decided to aim for a single month first, and to treat each extra month as a small celebration.

At 340 dollars a month, Priya calculated, one full month of basic costs would be in the account in about four months, which was sooner than she had feared. She circled the date on her calendar in pencil and wrote beside it a single, rather hopeful word, which was safe. Small as the target was, it gave her a feeling that she could not remember having before, which was the feeling of being slightly ahead of events.

Before the money grew, Mr Okafor wanted the rules for spending it written down, and so he asked Priya to make two lists. On the first went the true emergencies, which were a lost job, an urgent repair, a medical bill or a sudden journey to help family. On the second went everything that merely felt urgent, such as a sale, a holiday or a friend's birthday dinner, and a cushion spent on that list, he warned, will not be there for the first.

The emergency money, Mr Okafor said, should be kept in a place that is safe, separate from the account used for daily spending and available at short notice. It is not the place for risky investments, because the point of a cushion is that it will be there on the day it is needed, at the full value it had when it was saved. He also suggested that she give it a plain name, so that she would think twice before dipping into it for a sale.

There is no shame in spending the cushion on a genuine emergency, said Mr Okafor, because that is precisely what it was built to do, and nobody should feel guilty about it. What matters is what follows, which is that refilling it becomes the first call on the next few pay days, ahead of every other goal. Only when it is whole again, he said, should the money be allowed to return to its usual jobs.

Priya confessed that the sum she could manage to save seemed too small to be worth the bother, and Mr Okafor shook his head. The first goal, he said, is not the amount but the habit, since a person who saves a little every month has already become a saver, and the sums can grow as her pay does. An enormous plan that is never started is of no use to anybody, while a modest one that runs for years can quietly achieve a great deal.

Borrowing, Mr Okafor explained, is never free, since the lender charges interest, which is simply the price paid for using someone else's money. The cost grows with two things, the size of the rate and the length of time the debt is left unpaid, and a small rate on a large sum over many years can turn into a surprisingly heavy bill. Priya had always pictured debt as a number, but he asked her to picture it as a meter that keeps running.

To make it real, Mr Okafor chose a round example, which was a debt of 1,000 dollars at a rate of 20 in every hundred each year. If nothing were paid back, he said, the bill would grow by about 200 dollars in the first year, and in the second year the interest would be charged on the larger sum. Priya did the arithmetic twice, because the first answer seemed far too unkind to be true, and the second answer agreed with it.

The statement that Mr Okafor held up showed a minimum payment so small that it looked like a kindness. He explained that the small figure has a cost of its own, because when only the minimum is paid, most of each payment is swallowed by interest and the balance falls very slowly. A debt that could be cleared in a year, he said, can be made to last for many, and the lender, of course, earns interest on every month of the wait.

Not all debts are the same, said Mr Okafor, and the sensible questions are what the money is for and how much it will cost. Borrowing at a modest rate to gain a skill or to start a business may be a fair bargain, while borrowing at a punishing rate for things that lose their charm in a month is a bad one. Cards and short loans with very high rates, he added, deserve the most suspicion of all.

Shops had found a clever way to make prices feel smaller, Mr Okafor observed, which was to divide them into four easy payments and let the buyer forget the whole. Some of these offers cost nothing extra if every payment is made on time, while others carry fees or high interest when a date is missed, and the difference is hidden in small print. He taught her two questions to ask before agreeing to anything, namely what the total cost will be and what happens if she pays late.

One evening, after the others had left the studio, Marta showed Priya the balance on her credit card, and it was 1,800 dollars. She had been paying only the minimum each month for as long as she could remember, and she had never once worked out how long it would take to finish. She looked relieved rather than ashamed to say it aloud, as if the secret had been heavier than the debt.

That evening Priya made her own list, which took only a few minutes and gave her a sharp little shock. There was a card balance of 300 dollars at 22 in every hundred each year, left over from her last months as a student, and a student loan that charged only about four in every hundred. Seeing the two rates side by side, she understood at once that they were completely different animals, even though both were called debt.

For anyone with several debts, said Mr Okafor, the first step is to list every one of them with its balance and its interest rate. The minimum payment goes to all of them, so that nothing falls behind, but every spare dollar goes to the one with the highest rate, since that is the one that costs most to leave alone. When it is paid off, the same money moves to the next, and the whole list shrinks faster than it first seems possible.

A small cushion should come first, Mr Okafor advised, so that the next surprise does not push her straight back onto the card. After that, every spare dollar should attack the debt that charges the most, since paying off 22 in every hundred is a better return than any savings account is likely to offer. Priya would therefore keep her 200 dollars a month for the cushion and send the other 140 dollars to the card.

There is another method, Mr Okafor went on, which is to clear the smallest debt first regardless of its rate, in order to enjoy an early victory and gather momentum. It may cost a little more in interest than the first method, but if the encouragement of an early success keeps a person going, it will beat a better plan that is abandoned. The best method, he said, is the one a person will actually follow to the end.

After about three months of steady extra payments, Priya made the last payment on her card and watched the balance turn to zero. The effect was surprisingly physical, a loosening in her chest as though she had put down a bag that she had carried for so long that she had forgotten its weight. Mr Okafor said only that the money she had been sending to the card was now free for other jobs, and that each month's interest she no longer paid was a small gift to herself.

In many countries, said Mr Okafor, banks and landlords check a person's record of repaying debts and paying bills before they agree to deal with them, and a good record can mean lower rates on a future loan. It is built in the dullest way imaginable, by paying on time, month after month, and he advised Priya to set up reminders so that no bill was ever forgotten. He added that the details vary from one country to the next, so she should learn how it works where she lives.

Priya spent an hour that evening setting reminders for every bill and arranging automatic payments for the minimum amounts, so that a forgotten date could never damage her record. Mr Okafor added two more habits, which were to apply for credit only when she truly needed it, since many applications at once can worry a lender, and to read her own record yearly where the law allows. Nothing about it was exciting, he said, and that was the whole beauty of it, because boring habits are the ones that last.

In the early years of the shop, Mr Okafor told her, he had let certain neighbours take their groceries on trust and pay on Friday, and he kept a battered notebook with a small tick beside every payment. Without any formal training, he had created his own record of reliability, and he used it to decide whom to trust with larger orders. A bank, he said, does exactly the same thing on a far bigger scale, only with a computer instead of a pencil.

Looking rich and being secure are very different things, said Mr Okafor, and a great deal of spending is done only to impress people who are not paying attention. The expensive car, the latest clothes and the grand party disappear into the past, while the money kept in savings quietly keeps working in the future. He did not forbid treats, but he asked her to notice whether a purchase was for her own enjoyment or for somebody else's opinion.

Mr Okafor remembered two customers from the same year, one who arrived in an enormous gleaming car and the other on a bicycle that was older than Priya. The man with the car often asked to pay on Friday and sometimes on the Friday after, while the cyclist paid in full every time and, as everyone eventually discovered, owned the building he lived in. Wealth, said Mr Okafor, is what you keep and not what you show, and the two are very easily confused.

When Priya read her bank statement line by line, she found three small monthly charges that she had forgotten she was paying, which added up to 35 dollars. One was for a streaming service she watched twice a month, one for an app that she had opened only on the day she downloaded it, and one for a gym that she had visited just once. She cancelled the second and the third, saved 25 dollars a month and realised that the most expensive leaks are the ones that make no sound.

Mr Okafor's next tool was a waiting rule, which said that for any want above 50 dollars she must wait seven days before buying it. The rule does not forbid anything, he stressed, but it separates what you want for a moment from what you want for a while. Priya tried it that same afternoon on a green jacket that cost 90 dollars, wrote the date in her notebook and walked out of the shop with empty hands.

When the seven days had passed, Priya found that the jacket had quietly lost its glow, and that she could hardly remember why she had wanted it so badly. She moved the 90 dollars into her laptop account instead and felt a small, private pleasure that no shop had ever sold her. The rule, she noted in her book, had not made her stronger, but it had given her feelings time to settle.

Being careful, Mr Okafor insisted, is not the same as being mean, and the aim was never to spend nothing but to spend on the things that deserve it. After a week of thought, and from her wants money, Priya bought a sturdy pair of boots for 80 dollars, because she would wear them almost every day for years. Divided by the number of days, he pointed out, the cost came to almost nothing, whereas the cheap pair she had bought before had lasted a single winter.

Time, said Mr Okafor, is the saver's great ally, because money that grows can itself go on to grow, so that earlier gains produce later gains of their own. He called this compound interest, and compared it to a snowball that is slow to start but grows heavier with every turn. The principle is easy to say and hard to feel, so he promised that next week they would work through an example.

On the balcony stood a lemon tree that Mr Okafor had grown from a seed twenty years earlier, and he used it as a teacher. For the first few years it had hardly seemed to grow at all, he said, but each year's growth had built on the last, and now it gave him a basket of fruit every autumn. Money that earns interest and is left alone, he added, behaves in a similar way, with slow beginnings and generous endings for those who have the patience to wait.

Consider a hundred dollars that grows by five in every hundred each year, said Mr Okafor, and ask how much there is after ten years if nothing is added. After the first year there are 105 dollars, after the second a little over 110, and by the tenth year the sum has reached about 163, because each year's growth is earned on the earlier growth as well. He stressed that this is only an example, since real returns are never so smooth or certain.

Mr Okafor then asked her to imagine the same hundred dollars growing by a plain five dollars a year, with nothing built on top, which would give 150 dollars after a decade. The real figure was about 163, and the extra thirteen dollars was the work of earlier growth earning growth of its own. It looked like a trifle, but he asked her to watch what happened to the gap as the years went on.

Stretched over twenty years, the same hundred dollars would become about 265, and over thirty years about 432, which is more than four times the sum that was first put in. Mr Okafor drew the curve for her, flat at first and then rising steeply, and pointed out that the last ten years added far more than the first ten. Patience, he said, is the one ingredient that this kind of arithmetic cannot do without, and it costs nothing to supply.

The lesson of the snowball, Mr Okafor said, is that the number of years often matters as much as the amount, so a person who starts early has a large advantage over one who begins later. The reason is simply that early money has longer to grow, and the growth of the later years rests on the growth of the earlier ones. It is no reason to despair if one has started late, however, for the best moment to start is whenever the decision is finally made.

Time is not the only ingredient, Mr Okafor went on, because the rate of growth matters almost as much. Over thirty years a hundred dollars growing at two in every hundred a year becomes only about 181, while the same sum growing at five in every hundred becomes about 432, more than twice as much. Higher rates, he cautioned, usually come with higher risks, which was a subject for another week, but she should never ignore the rate she is being paid.

Mr Okafor then turned from a single lump sum to the more realistic case of a regular habit. If Priya added 100 dollars every month for ten years, she would put in 12,000 dollars of her own, and at the same example rate the total would grow to a little over 15,000. The difference of about 3,000 dollars was growth she had not had to earn with extra effort, and it belonged to her simply because she had begun.

That weekend Priya looked up the interest rate on her own savings and discovered that it was very low, while another bank offered several times as much for the same kind of account. Before moving anything she read the conditions with care, checking whether the higher rate lasted, whether there were fees and how well deposits were protected in her country. A better rate is only a bargain, Mr Okafor reminded her, when the money is just as safe as it was before.

At the end of the week Priya wrote three short lines under a small drawing of a tree, saying begin now, add something regularly and leave the money alone. Mr Okafor read them twice, nodded and observed that none of it was complicated, which was exactly the difficulty. The hard part of compounding, he said, is not the sum but the waiting, because the waiting has to be done on days when nothing seems to be happening.

There is a quiet force, Mr Okafor continued, which makes money kept in a drawer lose its power, and it is called inflation, meaning the general rise in prices over time. In many years it is only a few in every hundred, though it varies widely between countries and periods, so a sum that buys a basket of bread today will buy a smaller basket in the future. Safe savings that earn less than inflation therefore lose ground, which is a reason to think about long-term goals carefully.

When Mr Okafor first opened his shop, he told her, a loaf of bread had cost about one dollar, and when he finally closed the door for the last time the same loaf cost about three. He had written every new price on a card with a thick pen, and he remembered the sighs of his customers as they read each one. No single rise had been dramatic, he said, but together they had quietly changed what a dollar could do.

Many countries employ an official office to follow the prices of a typical basket of everyday goods and services, such as bread, rent, fuel and bus tickets. When the same basket costs three in every hundred more than it did a year earlier, inflation for that year is said to be three in every hundred. The figure varies widely between countries and between years, Mr Okafor noted, and it is only an average, so her own personal rate depends on what she actually buys.

Imagine, said Mr Okafor, that prices rise by three in every hundred each year and that Priya leaves 100 dollars in a drawer. After ten years the notes would be exactly as she left them, and yet they would buy only what about 74 dollars buy today, which is a loss that no one ever sees happening. Inflation is a thief that leaves no footprints, he said, and the first defence against it is to ask what your money is doing while it waits.

A savings account may pay two in every hundred a year, said Mr Okafor, and that sounds like a gain until prices are rising by three in every hundred. In such a year the number in her account grows while the amount it can buy shrinks, so she is a little poorer in everything but arithmetic. Economists call the difference between the two figures the real return, and it is the figure that actually counts.

Pay is affected in the same way, Mr Okafor added, so a wage that stays the same for five years is in effect a wage that has been cut. This is one reason why it is reasonable to ask for a raise when the work has grown, or the prices have, and why a job that never raises pay deserves a second look. Priya, who had never connected the two ideas, wrote them side by side on a single line of her notebook.

Inflation is not the enemy of everyone, said Mr Okafor, because a debt with a fixed payment becomes a little easier to carry when prices and wages rise around it. This is not an argument for borrowing, he added at once, since the lender takes account of expected inflation when setting the rate, and the interest still has to be paid on time. It is simply one of those facts that make the economy more complicated than a single rule can capture.

Priya went home and fetched the 120 dollars of cash that she had been keeping in a kitchen drawer, and paid it into her savings account. It was not a panic, Mr Okafor assured her, only a tidy-up, because money that is needed soon is right to stay safe even if it earns little. The lesson of inflation applied mainly to goals that were years away, where safety alone could slowly become a kind of risk.

Among the receipts in her envelope Priya found a grocery bill from her first month of tracking, and she bought exactly the same items that week to compare. The total was a few dollars higher, an increase so small that nobody would have mentioned it in conversation, yet unmistakable on paper. For the first time inflation was not a word in a lesson but a number in her own kitchen.

Safety has a price as well, said Mr Okafor, as they watched the sun go down behind the rooftops, because money kept only in the safest places can lose ground to prices over many years. He was not urging her to take reckless gambles, only to grasp that every choice, including the choice to do nothing, carries a cost on one side and a risk on the other. Next week, he promised, they would turn to the ways in which people try to make money grow, and to the dangers that accompany the attempt.

Saving and investing, said Mr Okafor, serve different purposes, since saving is for safety and for goals that lie close, while investing is for goals that lie many years away. When you invest, you put money into things like shares in companies, which may grow in value over time but may also fall, so there is no guarantee that you will get back what you put in. The wise approach, he said, is to use each tool for the job it suits.

To invest, Mr Okafor explained, is to put money into something that may earn more for you over time, and the simplest example is a share in a business. A share is a small piece of ownership, so when the business does well its price may rise and it may pay out part of the profit, while a poor year can push both in the other direction. Other examples are lending money to a government or a company, which is called a bond, and owning a building that can be rented out.

His first investment, Mr Okafor confessed, had not been in shares at all but in a set of new shelves for the shop, which let him stock twice as many goods and paid for themselves within two years. He pointed out that it had been a gamble all the same, since the money could just as easily have gone on shelves that nobody needed, and that he and Ada had spent many nights doing sums before they decided. An investment, he said, is always a decision made while some of the facts are still hidden from view.

An investment can reward its owner in two different ways, Mr Okafor said, and a clear mind needs to keep them apart. The first is that the price may rise over the years, so that what was bought for 100 dollars can later be sold for more. The second is that it may pay a regular income, such as a share of a company's profit or the rent from a building, and neither reward is ever guaranteed.

In investing, said Mr Okafor, the chance of a larger gain almost always comes with a larger risk, which means that the value will swing up and down more widely along the way. Anyone who promises a high return with no risk at all is either mistaken or dishonest, and the promise itself should make you more careful rather than less. He asked Priya to remember that sentence, because he said it could save her a great deal of money.

On a sheet of graph paper Mr Okafor drew two lines, one smooth and gently rising for a savings account and one jagged for a basket of shares. The jagged line has often ended higher over long periods in the past, but in a bad year it can fall by a fifth or more, and nobody can promise that the future will match it. She would have to decide, he said, whether she could bear the zigzags in order to have the chance of the climb.

Risk has two sides, Mr Okafor said, and a sensible person looks carefully at both of them before deciding anything. The first is what her life could afford, which depends on her income, her cushion, her debts and how soon she needs the money. The second is how much worry she could bear, because a plan she cannot sleep with is a plan she will eventually abandon, however good it looks on paper.

Mr Okafor set her a test that required nothing but her imagination, which was to picture an investment of 1,000 dollars dropping to 900 in a single month. Priya closed her eyes and tried to feel it honestly, and she decided that a fall of that size would worry her but not ruin her, while one twice as large would probably have her checking the screen constantly. Knowing that about herself in advance, he said, was worth more than any forecast about the markets.

On the back of an envelope Mr Okafor drew a ladder with four rungs and wrote a word beside each one. The first was a cushion, the second was the repayment of costly debt, the third was saving for goals that were near, and only the fourth was investing for the long term. The order was not a law of nature, he admitted, but it was a sensible order, since there is little point in chasing growth while a single surprise could knock you backwards.

That evening Priya copied the ladder into her notebook and coloured in the first two rungs, because her cushion of one month's costs was complete and her card was paid. She was now standing on the third, saving for the laptop and for the deposit that was still some years away. It was a satisfying sight, and what pleased her most was that every step had a reason that she could explain to anyone who asked.

Do not put all your eggs in one basket is an old saying, Mr Okafor remarked, and in money it has a name, which is diversification. If a person puts everything into a single company or a single idea, one failure can destroy the lot, whereas a spread of many different holdings means that no single disappointment is fatal. It does not remove risk altogether, but it does make the whole ride a good deal less frightening, and that matters because frightened people tend to make poor decisions.
