Two farmers used to sell vegetables at the back of his shop, Mr Okafor remembered, and one of them grew nothing but tomatoes. When a freak hailstorm flattened the field in a single afternoon, the tomato farmer had no harvest at all, whereas his neighbour, who grew five different crops, lost only one of them and sold the rest as usual. The second farmer was not cleverer or luckier, Mr Okafor said, only less dependent on the fortunes of any single crop.

Marta had a friend who had put all of his savings into the shares of a single company, simply because everyone at his work was talking about it. Mr Okafor listened and said that this is the most common way to take a big risk without realising it, since the whole of the friend's savings now depended on the fate of one business. Even a famous and respectable company can stumble, and a person who owns nothing else has nowhere to land.

There are at least three ways to spread money, Mr Okafor explained, and a careful investor considers all of them. The first is across many different companies, the second is across different kinds of investment, such as shares, bonds and cash, and the third is across different countries, whose economies do not always rise and fall together. The more varied the mix, the less any single disappointment can hurt, though some falls, he warned, affect almost everything at the same time.

An easy way of spreading money, Mr Okafor explained, is through a fund, which pools the savings of many people and uses them to buy a wide range of shares or other holdings. A type called an index fund simply follows a long published list of companies, so that its owner holds a small piece of many businesses without trying to pick the winners. He pointed out that such funds are common, but that she should read how each one works before she buys.

When Priya put money into a fund, Mr Okafor explained, she would receive a number of units in exchange, and each unit would be a tiny share of everything that the fund owned. The price of a unit rises and falls with the value of those holdings, so that she can see at any time what her share is worth, and in many places she can start with a small amount. The fund itself is run by a company that charges a fee for the work, which would matter a great deal in a week or two.

An index, Mr Okafor said, is nothing more mysterious than a published list of companies, such as the largest hundred or the largest five hundred in a country. An index fund buys all of them in the same proportions, so that nobody has to guess which one will win, and because no one is paid to choose, it usually costs far less than other funds. He was careful to add that it still rises and falls with the market it follows, and that spreading money is not the same as being safe.

Some fund managers choose investments one by one in the hope of beating the market, and in any given year some of them succeed. Studies in several countries, however, have found that over periods of ten years or more most of them fall behind a simple index once their higher fees are counted. This is no guarantee about the future, Mr Okafor said, but it is a good reason to be sceptical of anyone who claims to know the winners in advance.

Funds come in many kinds, Mr Okafor said, and the three main ones are easy to remember. A share fund holds small pieces of companies and usually swings the most, a bond fund holds loans to governments and companies and usually swings less, and a mixed fund holds some of each in a fixed proportion. Less swinging does not mean no risk, however, because bonds can lose value too, especially when the issuer fails or when interest rates rise.

When Priya asked him straight out what she should buy, Mr Okafor laughed and refused, explaining that he did not know her whole life and that nobody who did not should pretend to. What he could give her was a checklist of three things to look for, and she wrote them down: a broad spread across many holdings, low yearly costs and a plan simple enough to explain in one sentence. If she could not describe what she owned to a friend, he said, she probably should not own it.

Every fund and every adviser charges a fee, said Mr Okafor, and though it may look tiny, it is taken every year whether the investment does well or badly. A yearly charge of one in every hundred on ten thousand dollars is a hundred dollars, and because those dollars would otherwise have kept growing, the cost over decades is much greater than it looks. Priya was to ask about fees before she signed anything, and to prefer plain, low-cost choices where they were available.

Mr Okafor took the example of 10,000 dollars growing at five in every hundred a year for thirty years, before any costs are counted, which would give about 43,000 dollars. If a fee of one in every hundred is taken from the savings each year, the growth shrinks to four in every hundred, and the same thirty years produce only about 32,000. The fee looked like a rounding error, he said, yet it had taken about 11,000 dollars, roughly a third of all the growth.

Fees hide in more places than people expect, Mr Okafor warned, and the word cost can mean several different things. There is the charge made by the fund itself, the charge for buying and selling, the charge made by the platform that holds the account and sometimes a separate fee paid to an adviser. The only safe course, he said, is to ask for the total yearly cost in writing, expressed as a plain number, and to walk away from anyone who cannot or will not supply it.

The prices of investments rise and fall, Mr Okafor warned, and sometimes they fall sharply, as they have done many times in the past. A drop in value is a loss only on paper until the holder sells, but he was careful to add that no one can promise that prices will recover, or how long recovery will take. For that reason, he said, only money that she did not need soon should ever be placed where it might drop.

Looking back over the long history of markets, Mr Okafor said, one finds sharp falls of a third or more that arrived without much warning and sometimes took many years to repair. Some recoveries were swift, some were slow, and a few places never regained their old peaks within a human working life. History is therefore a teacher and not a promise, he said, and the best she could do was to prepare for a fall in advance and not to predict one.

The greatest danger in investing, said Mr Okafor, is often not the market but the investor, because fear when prices fall tempts people to sell at the bottom, and excitement when prices soar tempts them to buy at the top. The remedy is to decide on a plan in a calm moment, write it down, and follow it when the feelings come. A rule written on a quiet day is a good friend on a frightening one.

Mr Okafor then told her about his own worst mistake, which came when he was in his fifties and had put some savings into a broad fund. After a year in which it fell by a quarter, and with the newspapers full of gloom, he panicked and sold, turning a loss on paper into a loss in fact. Over the following two years the fund recovered most of its fall, and he had to watch it happen from the sidelines, which he said was a very effective teacher.

On a quiet evening, with no screen in sight, Priya wrote a plan on a small card, and it had only three lines. The first said how much she would invest each month, the second said how often she would look, and the third said what she would do if prices fell, which was to read the card and wait. She put it in her wallet, where it would be waiting for her on the most frightening day.

A price that is watched every day, Mr Okafor observed, turns every small wobble into a drama, and the investor who watches most closely is often the one who acts most foolishly. Priya decided that when she began to invest she would look at the balance on one marked day each month and leave her phone alone for the rest of the time. She suspected that the days she did not look would be no different from the days she did, except that she would feel a good deal calmer.

One calm way to invest, said Mr Okafor, is to put in the same fixed amount every month, whatever the news happens to be. In months when prices are high the money buys fewer units and in months when they are low it buys more, so the timing evens itself out, and the whole routine takes away the need to guess. It does not remove risk, but it removes a great deal of the worry, and it lets her get on with her life while the plan quietly does its work.

The right place for money, Mr Okafor said, depends on when it will be needed, so he told Priya to match each goal with a suitable tool. Money required within a few years should stay somewhere safe, because a drop at the wrong moment would leave no time to recover, while money for a distant goal can bear more ups and downs. There is no exact rule, but the habit of asking when she would need each sum was, he said, the best guide.

By now the Laptop account held 570 dollars, and Priya would need every cent of it in a few months. Mr Okafor told her that this was a perfect example of money with a near deadline, and that it should stay in a safe account where it earns very little but cannot suddenly shrink. The small gain from taking a risk, he said, is never worth the large pain of arriving at the shop with a smaller sum than she had planned.

Mr Okafor knew a young couple who had put their house deposit into shares because the market had been rising for years and the gains looked easy. In the year before they hoped to buy, prices fell by a fifth, and the deposit that they had counted on was suddenly thousands of dollars short. They waited three years for it to recover, and the house they wanted was bought by somebody else.

Between the near and the far there is a middle ground, Mr Okafor said, and goals that lie three to ten years away call for judgement and not a fixed rule. Many people use a mixture of safe money and growth money for such goals, and as the date approaches they move more and more of it to the safe side, so that a late fall does little damage. Priya's home deposit was exactly this kind of goal, and she wrote the thought beside it in pencil.

The most distant goals, Mr Okafor said, are the ones that suit investing best, and for Priya these were the freedom to care for her mother one day and, eventually, her own retirement. Money that will not be touched for thirty years or more has time to recover from several bad years, so it can usually bear more ups and downs than money needed in two. Even then, he added, nothing is certain, and the plan has to be revisited as the years go by.

One morning Ms Lin, her manager, mentioned in passing that the studio ran a retirement plan, and that it would add money to the account whenever an employee paid in some of her own. Priya had been given the leaflet in her first week and had never opened it, and she went red at the thought of how much she might have been missing. That evening she asked Mr Okafor what she ought to check before she signed up for anything at all.

Money that an employer adds to a plan, Mr Okafor said, is a form of extra pay, and it is seldom wise to refuse it. Priya read the leaflet with a pencil in her hand, underlining what the studio would add, what the yearly fees were, where the money would be invested and when she would be allowed to take it out. The rules in her country, she discovered, made the money hard to reach until she was much older, which was inconvenient and also, she admitted, rather the point.

Priya filled in the form on a Friday afternoon and chose to pay 100 dollars a month into the plan, taking it from the future box in her budget. The studio would add another 50 dollars each month, which meant that her account would grow by 150 dollars before a single day of growth had been earned. Mr Okafor, who had been waiting on the balcony for her news, said that it was the nearest thing to free money that he had seen in a lifetime of business.

Mr Okafor had noticed over thirty years that when people's pay rose, their spending rose to meet it as if by magic, and a decade later they were no better off than before. The remedy was to decide in advance that a fixed share of every raise, perhaps half, would go straight into the future box before the new money became part of ordinary life. Priya, whose pay would not rise for some time, wrote the rule down anyway, as a letter to a future self.

By the end of the month Priya had organised her money into three jars according to the time left before she would need it. The safe jar held the cushion and the laptop money, the middle jar held her home deposit, which she would manage with care as the date came nearer, and the long jar held her retirement plan. Each jar had its own account, its own rules and its own date, and for the first time she felt that her money was arranged like a well-run shop rather than scattered like loose change.

Scams, Mr Okafor warned, come in many costumes, but they share a few signs, namely a promise of quick and certain riches, pressure to act immediately and a request for secrecy. Any one of these should make her stop, and all three together should make her walk away, because an honest offer can survive a week's thought and a conversation with a friend. If she ever felt rushed, he said, that feeling itself was the warning, and the proper reply was always to slow down and ask someone she trusted.

Marta's cousin, a careful man by all accounts, had joined a scheme that promised to double his money in three months, and for the first few weeks it did exactly what it promised. The payments, however, came from the money paid in by newer members, not from any real business, and when new members stopped arriving the whole structure collapsed in a weekend. His savings of several years went with it, and he was too embarrassed to tell his own family for a month.

On a sheet of paper Mr Okafor drew a triangle with one person at the top and five people below, and then five more below each of those. If every member must find five new members, he said, twelve rounds of recruiting would need more than 240 million people, which is more than the population of many large countries. A scheme that depends on endless growth is therefore not a business at all, since the arithmetic guarantees that it must stop and that the last to join will lose.

Many scams, Mr Okafor said, arrive as a message that pretends to be from a bank or a delivery company, claiming that something is wrong and that she must act at once. The message asks for a password, a secret code or a click on a link, and the link leads to a copy of the real website whose only purpose is to collect what she types. The safe response is never to use the link or number in the message, but to close it and contact the real organisation by a number that she already knows.

Think about it from the other side, Mr Okafor said: if a person really owned a safe way to make huge profits, why would that person need your small savings? He or she could borrow from a bank at a low rate and keep every dollar of the gain, and the fact that they are asking you instead should tell you something. A guaranteed high return is therefore a warning, never a reason, and it echoes the sentence that Priya had written in her notebook about the seesaw.

Before any money moves, said Mr Okafor, she should make four checks, and the first is whether the seller is registered or licensed where she lives, which many countries let you look up on an official list. The second is to search the name together with the word complaints, the third is to ask for the details in writing, and the fourth is to give herself a week to think. An honest seller will not mind any of these, he said, and a dishonest one will find a reason why there is no time.

Nobody should feel stupid for being caught, Mr Okafor said, because scammers are professionals who study how to play on fear, hope, loneliness and the wish to be helpful, and clever people fall for them every year. If it happens, the right response is to tell the bank at once, to report the crime to the authorities and to tell a friend, because speed can sometimes save part of the money. Shame, he added, helps nobody except the thief, who is counting on the victim to stay silent.

In the autumn a nineteen-year-old intern named Tomi joined the studio, and in his second week he showed Priya an excited message on his phone. A stranger had promised to double any money he sent within a day, and Tomi, who had almost nothing saved, was already working out how much he could borrow. Priya recognised the three signs at once, and she asked him quietly to put the phone down and to give her five minutes.

Priya wrote three questions on a yellow sticky note, as Mr Okafor might have done, and handed it to Tomi across the desk. The questions were who is this person, who gains if I say yes and what happens if I wait a week, and none of them needed any expertise. Tomi read them twice, laughed in a shaky way, deleted the message, and admitted that he had been about to send his entire month's food money.

Priya spent the weekend closing the doors that thieves like to use, beginning with her passwords, which were three short ones that she used again and again. She replaced them with a different long password for every account, kept safe in a password manager that she could open with a single strong phrase, and she switched on the second step of sign-in wherever it was offered. It was dull work, as protection so often is, but it felt like locking a front door before a long journey.

Cutting spending has a limit, said Mr Okafor, since no one can spend less than nothing, but there is no such limit on what a person might earn. Building skills that others value, asking for fair pay when she has earned it and looking for better openings are all ways of raising income, and a bigger income gives more room for saving and for choice. Of all the things she could invest in, he said, her own ability was the one most likely to repay her.

Instead of guessing, Priya asked Ms Lin directly which skill would make her most useful to the studio, and the answer came without a pause. Simple animation, said Ms Lin, because clients kept asking for it and almost nobody on the team could do it well enough to satisfy them. Mr Okafor was delighted when he heard, and said that the best skill to learn is the one that somebody is already begging for.

Priya enrolled in an eight-week animation course that met in the evenings and cost 150 dollars, a sum she paid from her fun money over two months so that the plan itself was left undisturbed. She promised herself three hours of practice each week, which meant giving up some television and one lazy Sunday morning, and she wrote the sacrifice in her notebook so that she would remember what it was for. Mr Okafor said that nothing she could buy would repay her better than her own ability, provided that she actually used it.

Mr Okafor liked to look at learning as an investment, so he helped her to work out a simple sum. If the course eventually led to only 100 dollars more each month, it would repay its cost of 150 dollars in less than two months, and the extra income would then continue for as long as the skill was useful. He added at once that nobody could promise such a result, but that even a modest chance of it made the course a far better bet than most things for sale.

Six weeks into the course, Ms Lin trusted Priya with a small job, a moving logo for a client's website that would normally have gone to an outside freelancer. Priya worked on it for three evenings, made two mistakes that she fixed before anyone saw them and delivered it a day early. The client was pleased, and Ms Lin said so in front of the whole team, which was the first time in her working life that Priya had been praised for something she had learned on her own.

Asking for a raise, said Mr Okafor, is a skill with three parts, and most people neglect the first. The first is to gather evidence of work done, with figures wherever possible, the second is to choose a calm moment, and the third is to name a number, since a vague request is easy to refuse. Priya made a list of what she had finished since February, from new logos to a client's letter of thanks, and she was surprised at how long it was.

On a quiet Thursday Priya asked Ms Lin for a raise of 150 dollars a month, handed over her list and then stopped talking, which Mr Okafor had told her was the hardest and most important part. Ms Lin read the list slowly, said that she could not manage the full amount, and offered 100 dollars a month from the next pay day with a fresh review in six months. Priya said thank you, shook her hand and walked back to her desk with her knees feeling oddly weak.

Before the first larger payment arrived, Priya set up her automatic transfers again, sending 50 dollars of the extra 100 straight to her deposit savings and leaving the other 50 for her ordinary life. It felt a little strange to give herself permission to enjoy half of her good news, as though she needed to be forgiven for it. Mr Okafor said that was precisely the balance he wanted, because a rule that has no pleasure in it will not survive the first bad month.

A friend who owned a small cafe asked Priya to design its new menu for 80 dollars, and she agreed, working on it over two weekends. Mr Okafor approved of the extra income but asked her three questions, which were whether it was worth her time, whether it would tire her and whether the tax office needed to hear about it. She wrote the amount in her records on the day it arrived, because earnings that are never recorded have a way of becoming trouble later.

After a month of courses, a menu and a raise, Priya was tired, and Mr Okafor looked at her carefully before he spoke. More income is a good thing, he said, but only if it does not cost her health, rest and friends, and only if her spending does not rise to swallow it. She took the next weekend completely off, with no screen and no work, and discovered that rest, like a good habit, pays back more than it costs.

Insurance, explained Mr Okafor, is a way of sharing risk, since many people pay small regular amounts and the few who suffer a serious loss are helped from the common pool. It is best used for events that would be too large for her to bear alone, such as a major illness, a car accident or the loss of a home, and not for small things she could easily pay herself. He told her to read the terms carefully and to compare more than one offer.

Mr Okafor explained insurance with a village of 1,000 neighbours, each owning a bicycle worth 300 dollars, of which about ten are stolen in an average year. If each neighbour pays three dollars into a common pot, the pot holds 3,000 dollars, which is exactly enough to replace the ten stolen bicycles, and each owner has swapped a rare large loss for a small certain cost. A real insurer has expenses and needs a profit, he added, so real prices are higher, but the principle of sharing a risk among many is exactly the same.

Mr Okafor gave her a simple test to apply before she bought any insurance, which was to ask what would happen if the loss arrived tomorrow. If she could pay for it from her cushion without real pain, she probably needed no cover, whereas a loss that would wreck her finances for years deserved serious protection. A cracked phone screen was therefore a matter for the cushion, he said, and a major illness or the loss of a home was a matter for an insurer.

He named five common kinds of cover, which were health, home or contents, travel, life and income, and he explained each in a sentence. Life cover matters mainly to people whom others depend on, while income cover replaces part of a wage if illness stops someone from working, and health cover varies enormously from one country to another. Which of them she needed, he said, depended on her country, her job and her family, and some of them might already be provided by the state or by her employer.

On a winter night a pipe had burst above the store room of the shop, Mr Okafor remembered, and by morning half the stock stood in an inch of cold water. Ada had chosen a policy that specifically covered water damage, after reading every line of the terms, and the insurer paid for most of what was ruined within a month. Without it, he said quietly, the shop would very probably have closed within the year.

Two words, Mr Okafor said, were worth learning before she signed anything, and the first was premium, which is the regular price paid for the cover. The second was excess, sometimes called the deductible, which is the part of any claim that she pays herself before the insurer pays the rest. A higher excess usually means a lower premium, so a person with a good cushion can often save money by choosing it, while a person with no cushion would be wise to pay more and keep the excess small.

Most disputes about insurance, said Mr Okafor, arise from things that the buyer never read, and so he asked her to look at three parts of any policy before she paid. The first was what is left out, which is often listed under exclusions, the second was the limit on each claim and the third was how and how quickly to make a claim. If any sentence puzzled her, she was to ask the seller to explain it in plain words, and to write down the answer.

Priya compared three offers, read each policy with her pencil in hand and chose simple cover for her belongings and her bicycle at 12 dollars a month. She picked an excess of 50 dollars, because her cushion could easily pay that much, and she noticed that the cheapest offer excluded bicycles that were left locked outside. It was a small decision, but she signed with the pleasant feeling of having understood every line of it.

Some salespeople, Mr Okafor warned, offer packages that mix insurance and investing in a single product and describe them as the best of both worlds. They can be perfectly suitable for some people, but they often carry high fees and long commitments and are hard to compare with anything else, so he preferred to keep the two jobs apart. Insurance should do the work of protection, he said, and growth should be arranged separately, where she can see exactly what each part costs.

Priya circled the renewal date in pencil on her calendar, because Mr Okafor had told her that insurers sometimes raise the price quietly for people who never check. A cover that was right last year might be wrong this year, he said, and a yearly comparison takes an hour and may save a good deal of money. When someone eventually depended on her, a partner, a child or a parent, he added, the whole question would need to be thought through again from the beginning.

Taxes, said Mr Okafor, are a fact of earning, and the rules differ so much between countries that he could only give her a general outline. She should learn how her own country treats income and savings, keep her papers in order and find out whether any official savings accounts give her a legal advantage. When the matter is complicated, it is worth paying a qualified person for advice, and a small fee can easily save a larger mistake.

Taxes, Mr Okafor said, are the price that a society pays for the things that its members share, such as roads, schools, hospitals and courts, and few enjoy paying them but most would miss what they buy. The rules differ so much between countries that he could not describe hers, so Priya's task was to find out which taxes were taken from her pay, which she paid herself and which forms she must file. The information was published by her government, he said, in a form that anyone could read with patience.

On the first evening of the week Priya took out the pay slip that had made her anxious in February, and this time she read it line by line, with a pencil. At the top was her gross pay, the full amount her employer owed her, and below it a short list of tax and other deductions that were taken off before a cent reached her account. What remained at the bottom was her net pay, the only number she had ever really watched, and she was glad to see at last where the difference had gone.

Deadlines, Mr Okafor said, were the part of taxes that caught most people out, because they are firm and the penalties for missing them can be heavy even when no tax is owed. Priya looked up the dates that applied to her, wrote each one in her calendar with a reminder a fortnight earlier and made a folder in which she would keep a copy of everything she sent. The folder was empty for now, but she liked the look of it, in the way that one likes a clean notebook.

Ada, who had kept the shop's accounts for thirty years, invited Priya into her kitchen and showed her a system that had never failed, which was one box for receipts, one folder for letters and fifteen minutes each month. In the box went every receipt that might matter later, and in many countries receipts for work expenses can reduce a tax bill, though she advised Priya to check the rules where she lived. The system was so simple that Priya almost laughed, until she saw the shelf of thirty neat folders behind her.

Priya added the 80 dollars from the cafe menu to her records and then looked up what the rules said about extra income, which took a little patience and two official websites. In her country, she discovered, small amounts still had to be reported, though they were taxed in a simple way, and she made a note in her calendar for the end of the year. If the matter had been complicated, Mr Okafor reminded her, the sensible thing would have been to pay a qualified person a small fee for a clear answer.

Mr Okafor also advised that she keep a simple record of her accounts, her insurance and her important papers in one safe place, and tell someone she trusts where to find it. If she were ever ill or absent, or if the worst happened, her family would not need to search in a panic. In many countries, he added, a short will is also wise, though the rules differ and a local professional can explain them.

Priya sat down with a pen and wrote a list of everything that mattered, including her bank, her savings, her retirement plan and her insurance, with the name and contact details beside each. She was careful to leave out every password, which Mr Okafor said should never be written in such a list, and she sealed the page in an envelope. Then she rang her mother and told her exactly where it was, which led to a long and surprisingly tender conversation.

Borrowing from Ada's system, Priya began a monthly money check that took fifteen minutes and a cup of tea. She looked at her balances, confirmed that each automatic transfer had arrived, scanned the statements for charges that she did not recognise and saved a copy of her important papers in a second place. Most months nothing was wrong, which she came to see as the whole purpose, since the one month in which something was wrong would be caught early.

When the work was done, Priya lined up a box, a folder and a sealed envelope on her shelf and stood back to look at them. It was not an exciting sight, but it gave her a kind of calm she had never felt in February, when her whole money life had been a cloud of worry and one pay slip. Order, she wrote in her notebook, is not the enemy of freedom but one of its quietest forms.

Before any substantial purchase, said Mr Okafor, she should examine the total cost over time and not only the monthly payment, because sellers love to speak of the second and say little about the first. A modest payment spread across many years may conceal a great deal of interest, and the purchase itself may demand insurance, repairs and fuel besides. The question to ask, he said, is what it will cost altogether, and whether the object justifies that sum.

A price on a sign, Mr Okafor said, is only the first line of the bill, and he asked Priya to write down everything else that comes with a home. There is the deposit, the legal and administrative fees, the taxes that some countries charge on the purchase itself, the insurance and the repairs, which come sooner or later to every roof, boiler and drain. Many careful buyers have been taken by surprise by the last item, he said, and a sum set aside every year for it is rarely wasted.

Mr Okafor showed her how a longer loan can look kinder than it is, using 10,000 dollars borrowed at six in every hundred a year. Repaid over three years, the payment is about 304 dollars a month and the interest comes to about 950 dollars, while over five years the payment falls to about 193 dollars but the interest rises to about 1,600. The lower monthly figure feels like relief, he said, and it costs about 650 dollars for the privilege.

Whether to rent or buy a home has no single answer, said Mr Okafor, since it depends on the local prices, on the length of time she expects to stay and on her own tastes and plans. Buying brings costs that are easy to forget, among them repairs, taxes, fees and the loss of flexibility, while renting means that the money goes to a landlord but allows easy movement. The sensible course is to compare the full costs on paper for her own situation and to seek advice before signing.

Mr Okafor and Ada had rented the shop for ten years before they bought it, and they did so only when they were sure that they would stay for a long time. A friend of theirs bought a flat in a hurry, moved to another city after two years and lost a good deal of money in selling fees. A short stay, said Mr Okafor, gives a home no time to repay its costs, and time is the hidden question in every choice between renting and buying.

Priya looked at a listing for a small flat near the river and then asked herself, as Mr Okafor had taught her, how long she was sure that she would stay in this city. The honest answer was that she did not yet know, since the animation course had opened doors that might lead anywhere. She decided to keep renting for now and to go on saving toward the deposit, so that the choice would be hers whenever the answer became clear.

When Priya mentioned that she sometimes dreamed of a car, Mr Okafor handed her a pencil and asked her to add up its true yearly cost, including fuel, insurance, repairs, parking and the value that it loses as it ages. The total was a good deal higher than she had guessed, and it made the bicycle, the bus pass and the occasional taxi look like small wonders of economy. If she did need a car one day, he said, a reliable older one, whose steepest fall in value has already been paid by someone else, is usually the wiser buy.

There are times when professional help is valuable, said Mr Okafor, but the quality of advisers varies, and she should ask how any adviser is paid before she listens to a word. Someone who earns money from selling a particular product has a reason to recommend it, so she should look for a person who explains the choices plainly, shows the fees in writing and welcomes her questions. A good adviser is happy to be asked, he said, and a poor one grows impatient.

On a small card Mr Okafor wrote four questions for Priya to carry to any meeting with an adviser. The first asked how the adviser was paid, the second asked for the total yearly cost, the third asked whether the adviser was bound to put her interests first and the fourth asked for the answers in writing. A good adviser, he said, answers all four calmly and sometimes even thanks you for asking, while a bad one suddenly remembers another appointment.

After her first meeting with a real adviser, a polite woman who answered all four questions without a blink, Priya made a rule that she would never break, which was never to sign anything in the meeting itself. She took the papers home, slept on them and read them again in the morning, when the pressure of a pleasant conversation had faded and only the words remained. In the end she signed nothing, because she found that she did not need the product, and she felt proud of the strength of that small refusal.

Priya and Leo had been together for four months, and in all that time the subject of money had come up only when a bill arrived. Over two cups of tea one Sunday they finally said aloud what each of them earned, what each owed and what each hoped for, and Priya found that the awkwardness lasted ten minutes and the relief far longer. Mr Okafor, hearing of it, said that the habit of honest talk is easiest to start when nothing is wrong.

Leo earned less than Priya, so they agreed that fairness did not have to mean splitting every bill in half, and that sharing costs in proportion to pay might suit them both better. They opened a small joint account for the costs they truly shared, such as food and holidays, and each of them kept a pot of money that was entirely their own, to be spent without explanation. Mr Okafor said that a little privacy with money often makes a couple's life calmer, and that the habit costs almost nothing.

Leo spent freely and Priya saved carefully, and for a few weeks the difference produced small arguments that were never really about money at all. They solved it by asking each other why, since Leo had grown up in a house where money was scarce and had learned to enjoy it while it lasted, while Priya had grown up learning to worry. They then chose two goals to share, agreed on one evening a month to talk about them over supper and found that the arguments quietly stopped.

Her younger brother Dev, who was still a student, rang one evening to ask whether he could borrow 200 dollars for his books until the end of the term. Priya wanted to help him very much, and at the same time she remembered every story that Mr Okafor had told her about friendships bruised by borrowed money. She said that she would call him back in an hour, and went to ask the one person who would understand.

Lend only what you could afford to lose, said Mr Okafor, say clearly whether it is a gift or a loan, and write down the amount and the date, because even the best memories drift apart. Priya lent Dev the 200 dollars from her fun money, wrote a friendly note with the date by which she hoped to be repaid and told herself that she could live with it if the money never came back. Dev, to her surprise, was touched by the note and repaid her a week early.

Giving, Mr Okafor said, can be a proper part of a plan, whether it means helping family, supporting a cause or simply being generous at a festival. Setting aside an amount on purpose means that generosity is a decision, not an accident, and that it does not leave her short when her own bills fall due. Many people find that thoughtful giving brings them as much satisfaction as anything else they buy.

One evening Priya admitted that the holidays and gadgets of her friends, as they appeared online, made her feel she was falling behind. Mr Okafor reminded her that she saw only what others chose to show and knew nothing of their debts, their worries or their goals, and that a life copied from someone else's picture is unlikely to fit. The only fair comparison, he said, was between her own situation now and the plan she had made.

Advertising, Mr Okafor said, is a very skilled craft whose purpose is to make a person feel that what she has is not quite enough, and that the missing piece can be bought. Priya muted three accounts that made her feel behind and wrote down what enough would look like for her, with numbers for her cushion and her deposit and a list of the things she loved. It was a surprisingly short list, and she kept it where she could see it.

During a big sale at the end of the month Priya forgot her waiting rule and came home with 140 dollars' worth of things that she could not even have named a week later. That night she sat among the bags feeling that all her progress had been wasted, and the old word worried returned to the front of her mind. Mr Okafor listened without a trace of surprise, and then he told her about another mistake of his own, which had cost far more than a sale.

Years earlier, Mr Okafor confessed, he had lent a friend 2,000 dollars for a business without writing a single word down, and he never saw the money again, nor, in the end, the friend. The only real failure, he said, is to hide a mistake or to give up because of one, and he suggested that Priya keep a small log with three columns, which were the date, what happened and the lesson. Priya wrote her first line that night, with a rueful smile, and closed the book feeling lighter than she had when she opened it.

A plan is not a statue, said Mr Okafor, but a living thing that should be reviewed at least once a year and whenever life changes in a major way. A new job, a move, a marriage, a child or the end of a debt are all reasons to ask whether the old goals and amounts are still suitable. He suggested that she choose a date, such as her birthday, and treat it as an annual appointment with her own future.

In the first week of December, exactly as planned, Priya bought her laptop and paid the full 600 dollars from the account that she had named for it ten months earlier. She did not borrow a cent, and she did not touch her cushion, which was the whole point of having kept the two apart. On the wall above her kitchen table, in pencil, she ticked the first of her three goals and felt a quiet, steady pride that was quite different from excitement.

On a fresh page of the notebook Priya listed what the year had built, and the entries came in a quiet column. There was no card debt any more, there was a cushion equal to one month of her basic costs, there was a deposit jar that grew every month and there was a retirement plan that the studio helped to fill. None of it would have made a headline, yet in February the whole column had been blank, and she looked at it for a long time.

With her notebook open beside the plan's leaflet, Priya compared each investment option against the three-point list that she had written months before. One option was a broad index fund with low yearly costs, and she found that she could explain it to herself in a single sentence, which none of the others allowed. She chose it, set the amount to continue every month, put her three-line plan card back in her wallet and promised herself to look at the balance only on the marked day.

A plan is a living thing, Mr Okafor had said, and Priya proved it by rubbing out the finished laptop goal and writing a new one in its place, a spring journey to see her mother. The 60 dollars a month that had been going to the laptop would now go to the journey, and the amount and the date were written beside it exactly as before. She also moved the next review into her calendar for the following December, with a small drawing of a tree beside it.

As the year drew toward its close, Mr Okafor asked Priya to turn everything she had learned into a short list of personal rules, written in her own words and limited to a single page. A rule that she had thought through herself, he said, would be far easier to follow than any advice borrowed from someone else, and the rules of two people would never be exactly alike. Her list was plain, and it began with the sentence that money is a tool for choices.

The page that Priya finished that week had eight short rules on it, and each one sounded like her. “Money is a tool for choices,” she had written, “and I will know where mine goes, I will pay myself first, I will keep a cushion, I will borrow with care and I will let time do its work.” The last two lines said that she would slow down at every offer and look at the whole plan once a year, and she signed the bottom of the page like a letter.

Money, said Mr Okafor as the evening turned cool, is only one of the ingredients of a good life, and not even the most important, for health, friendship, meaningful work and free time are worth at least as much. The purpose of managing it well is to protect those other treasures and to leave room for them, never to replace them. A person who forgets this may be wealthy by the numbers yet impoverished in every respect that truly matters.

By January Tomi had been at the studio for a few months, and one lunchtime he asked Priya, a little shyly, how a person begins with money when there is hardly any of it. Priya laughed aloud, because she suddenly saw herself on a balcony in February with a pay slip in her hand, and she saw that she had become the neighbour with a few ideas to share. She told him that she would not give him a lecture, only one idea a week, if he would be willing to try each one.

Priya passed her page of rules to Tomi on the balcony and said that it was only a starting point, because every life is different and each person must write the rules that suit their own. You can do the same: set your goals, watch where your money goes, build a cushion, borrow with care, invest patiently and let time do its work. This book is general information and is not personal financial advice, so check the rules where you live and ask a qualified professional about your own situation before you make big decisions.
